title: GOD SENT HORNETS AHEAD OF THEM—AND ISRAEL DISCOVERED THE BATTLE WAS NEVER THEIRS ALONE
paragraphs: GOD SENT HORNETS AHEAD OF THEM—AND ISRAEL DISCOVERED THE BATTLE WAS NEVER THEIRS ALONE

Joshua 24:12 contains one of Scripture’s strangest pictures of divine deliverance: before Israel could boast about swords, strength, or strategy, God reminded them that He had already gone ahead of them.
There is something almost unsettling about Joshua 24:12.
Not because it is difficult to understand.
Because it is difficult to forget.
God is reminding Israel of everything He had done for them when He suddenly says:
“And I sent the hornet before you, which drave them out from before you, even the two kings of the Amorites; but not with thy sword, nor with thy bow.” — Joshua 24:12, KJV
Read that final sentence again.
“Not with thy sword, nor with thy bow.”
Israel carried swords.
Israel carried bows.
Israel still had battles to face.
And yet God deliberately interrupted their memory of conquest to make something painfully clear:
You did not save yourselves.
The Hebrew makes the image even more vivid.
וָאֶשְׁלַח לִפְנֵיכֶם אֶת־הַצִּרְעָה
Va’eshlaḥ lifneikhem et-hatzir‘ah.
“And I sent before you the hornet.”
The word translated “hornet” is הַצִּרְעָה — hatzir‘ah — from צִרְעָה (tsir‘ah), referring to a hornet or stinging insect.
But notice the phrase before it:
לִפְנֵיכֶם — lifneikhem.
“Before you.”
Ahead of you.
Before Israel arrived, God was already at work.
Before their feet reached the battlefield...
before swords were raised...
before arrows were released...
before anyone could stand over conquered territory and congratulate himself...
God had gone ahead.
That is the part some of us desperately need to hear.
Because you may be standing in front of something right now that looks bigger than you.
A battle in your family.
A temptation you are ashamed to admit still knows your name.
A financial burden that follows you into bed.
A marriage carrying wounds nobody sees.
A child you keep praying will come home to God.
A private sin you keep promising Jesus you will never touch again... until you do.
Maybe you are exhausted because you have been trying to fight spiritually with nothing but your own sword and bow.
More discipline.
More promises.
More determination.
“I’ll fix myself.”
“I’ll do better this time.”
“I’ll become stronger.”
And perhaps the most dangerous sentence of all:
“I can handle this.”
Israel had weapons.
But Israel's weapons were never Israel's Savior.
Neither are yours.
Joshua 24 is not primarily a motivational speech about Israel discovering hidden strength. It is covenant history. Joshua gathers the tribes and rehearses what God has done.
Again and again, God is the acting subject.
“I took...”
“I gave...”
“I sent...”
“I plagued...”
“I brought...”
“I delivered...”
“I destroyed...”
“I would not hearken...”
“I delivered you...”
“I sent...”
“I gave...”
Then comes the devastating conclusion:
“Not with thy sword, nor with thy bow.”
God was stripping away the illusion of self-salvation.
And centuries later, the Gospel would expose that illusion even more completely.
Because our deepest enemy was never merely an Amorite king standing outside a city.
Our deepest problem runs through the human heart.
Sin.
Guilt.
Rebellion.
Death.
Separation from God.
And no sword you possess can cut sin out of your soul.
No amount of moral effort can purchase forgiveness.
No religious performance can make the guilty innocent before a holy God.
You cannot outwork your need for grace.
You cannot impress God into forgiving you.
You cannot bleed enough to pay for your own rebellion.
So Someone else bled.
That is where every road of Scripture ultimately finds its center in Jesus Christ.
At Calvary, humanity's greatest victory did not look like victory.
The Messiah was mocked.
Stripped.
Rejected.
Nailed to wood.
Blood ran from His wounds.
His followers scattered.
His enemies thought the story was ending.
Then Jesus cried:
Τετέλεσται.
Tetelestai.
“It is finished.” — John 19:30
Not, “I am finished.”
“It is finished.”
The work the Father had given Him reached its appointed completion.
The debt of sin was not answered by your sword.
Not by your bow.
Not by your religious résumé.
Not by your ability to appear righteous while hiding what is really happening inside you.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
And salvation is received by grace through faith, producing a transformed life that belongs to Him.
Maybe that is why this strange verse about hornets can hit so deeply.
Because underneath all our polished Christianity, many of us are still trying to become our own savior.
We pray...
then panic as though everything depends on us.
We surrender...
then quietly take everything back.
We sing about grace...
then punish ourselves for sins Christ calls us to confess and forsake.
We say Jesus is Lord...
while protecting one locked room in the heart where we do not want Him entering.
And sometimes God allows us to reach the end of our strength because the end of self-sufficiency can become the beginning of surrender.
But Joshua 24:12 should not be turned into a promise that God will miraculously remove every difficulty before Christians encounter it.
Israel still fought battles.
Believers still suffer.
Faithful Christians still experience persecution, sickness, grief, unanswered questions, and death.
Jesus never promised His disciples a painless road.
He promised something better than a painless road.
Himself.

The “hornet” of Joshua 24 has also generated discussion among interpreters about precisely how the language should be understood. The text itself says God sent the tsir‘ah before Israel, and similar language appears in Exodus 23:28 and Deuteronomy 7:20. Some interpreters understand literal hornets; others have proposed that the imagery represents terror, panic, or another providential means by which God drove Israel's enemies away.
We should not pretend Scripture tells us more than it does.
But we should not miss what Scripture plainly emphasizes.
God acted.
God went before them.
God delivered.
And Israel was forbidden to write itself into the story as its own redeemer.
That truth becomes breathtaking when seen through the Gospel.
Your testimony, if you belong to Christ, will never ultimately be:
“Look what I accomplished.”
It will be:
“Look what Jesus did.”
I was guilty...
and He offered forgiveness.
I was wandering...
and He called me to repentance.
I was enslaved to sin...
and Christ became my Redeemer.
I was trying to hide...
and grace found me in the darkness.
I thought my scandal would become the final chapter.
Jesus started writing another one.
That does not mean sin does not matter.
Grace is not God pretending rebellion is harmless.
The cross proves exactly the opposite.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God went to Calvary.
Yet God's mercy is so astonishing that sinners who repent and trust in Christ can be forgiven, reconciled, adopted, and transformed.
That is scandalous grace.
Peter knew something about it.
He promised loyalty to Jesus and then denied knowing Him.
Not once.
Three times.
Imagine carrying that memory.
Imagine hearing your own voice saying, “I know not the man.”
Imagine watching Jesus die knowing that when courage was demanded from you, fear won.
Peter had his scandal.
Then the risen Jesus came looking for Peter.
Jesus did not call Peter's denial righteousness.
He restored a repentant disciple.
“Feed my sheep.”
Failure was not allowed to become Peter's final identity.
Grace rewrote what shame wanted to make permanent.
Maybe your scandal looks different.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe people at church see the version of you that knows when to smile, when to raise your hands, when to say “God is good,” and when to post a Bible verse.
But Jesus sees beneath the presentation.
He sees the browser history.
He sees the bitterness.
He sees the secret relationship.
He sees the envy.
He sees what alcohol cannot numb.
He sees the resentment you call discernment.
He sees the pride hiding beneath ministry.
He sees the prayers you stopped praying.
He sees the tears you wipe away before anybody enters the room.
And still the Gospel invitation is not, “Clean yourself sufficiently, then come.”
It is:
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Stop hiding.
Bring the sin into His light.
You do not need another mask.
You need a Savior.
Perhaps you have been asking God to send “hornets” against everything around you while He is exposing something within you.
Perhaps the enemy you desperately want defeated is not only the circumstance in front of you.
Maybe pride has to die.
Maybe bitterness has to be surrendered.
Maybe pornography has to be confessed and abandoned.
Maybe forgiveness has to replace revenge.
Maybe the secret has to come into the light.
Maybe your plans have become an idol.
Maybe Jesus does not merely want to change your situation.
He wants you.
All of you.
This is where Joshua's speech eventually leads.
“Now therefore fear the LORD, and serve him in sincerity and in truth...” — Joshua 24:14
Deliverance demands a response.
Grace is not permission to keep our idols.
Grace calls us away from them.
Joshua eventually declares:
“As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.” — Joshua 24:15
That famous declaration makes more sense when we remember what came before it.
Joshua was not saying, “Look how strong my family is.”
He had just spent the chapter saying:
Look what God has done.
That changes everything.
Christian obedience is not an attempt to make Jesus save us.
It is the response of people who know they desperately needed saving.
So what are you still carrying as though everything depends on your sword?
What are you still trying to conquer without surrendering to Christ?
What shame are you still hiding because you think Jesus will love the edited version of you more than the truth?
He already knows.
The question is whether you will finally stop running.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes honesty begins when somebody finally stops pretending.

And if Christ has already brought you through something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what He did. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to remind another exhausted believer that their story is not over.
Not because every day will feel dramatic, but because another day may come when the battle looks enormous and your strength feels embarrassingly small.
Come back and remember:
“Not with thy sword, nor with thy bow.”
And yes—even send it to someone who does not believe yet.
Let them see what Christianity actually announces:
Not that good people climb their way to God.
But that God, in His mercy, came to rescue sinners through Jesus Christ.
Not as a payment for God's blessing.
Not as a way to purchase favor from Him.
God's grace cannot be bought.
And there is more available even without purchasing anything.
But before you leave, remember the strange little detail Joshua refused to let Israel forget.
The hornets went ahead.
The sword was not the savior.
The bow was not the savior.
Israel was not the savior.
And neither are you.
There will be battles in which God calls you to stand.
There will be obedience that costs you something.

There will be sins you must forsake, relationships you must repair, temptations you must resist, truth you must speak, crosses you must carry, and days when faithfulness feels like walking through fire.
But you never graduate from needing grace.
The Christian life begins with Christ.
It continues through Christ.
It ends in Christ.
So put down the fantasy that you can redeem yourself.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the failure.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the broken pieces you have been hiding behind your back.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Jesus.
Because the same God who would not allow Israel to credit its sword for deliverance will not allow us to place the crown of salvation upon human strength.
That crown belongs to Jesus.
And perhaps the sentence you need to carry into tonight is simply this:
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending when your life has been surrendered to Jesus Christ.
